title: P Pairs With The Smallest Worst Gap
statement:
You get an array nums and a number p. Form exactly p pairs of elements. No index may be used in more than one pair.

The gap of a pair is the absolute difference of its two values. Among all ways to form the p pairs, make the largest gap as small as possible, and return that largest gap. If p = 0, return 0.

examples.why: Sorted: 1 2 3 7 8 9. Pairs (1,2), (3,7), (8,9) have gaps 1, 4, 1. Grabbing the two cheapest pairs (1,2) and (7,8) first leaves 3 and 9 with a gap of 6.
The two 5s pair up with gap 0. The 20 stays unused.

hints: Sort first. In an optimal answer, can you always pair neighbours in sorted order?
Turn the question around: for a fixed limit D, can you form p pairs whose gaps are all at most D? If D works, every larger D works too.
To test a limit D, walk the sorted array: if nums[i+1] − nums[i] ≤ D, take that pair and jump by 2, otherwise move by 1. Binary search for the smallest D that yields at least p pairs.

explain.intuition:
After sorting, crossing pairs never help: if a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ d, pairing (a,b) and (c,d) is never worse than (a,c)/(b,d) or (a,d)/(b,c). So every pair can be two neighbours in sorted order.

Now guess the answer. For a limit D, greedily scan the sorted array and take a neighbour pair whenever its gap fits. Taking the leftmost pair that fits is safe: skipping it can only leave you with fewer usable elements on the right. The number of pairs you get grows as D grows, so binary search over D from 0 to max − min finds the smallest limit that gives p pairs. It is the same move as tuning a debounce delay: test a value, and the yes/no answer tells you which half to keep.
steps: For a middle value D, count pairs greedily: at index i, if nums[i+1] − nums[i] ≤ D count one and set i += 2, else i += 1.
If the count reaches p, the answer is at most D: search left. Otherwise search right.
pitfalls: Taking the p smallest neighbour gaps without checking that they do not share an element. Two overlapping cheap pairs cannot both be used, as the first example shows.
Moving by 1 instead of 2 after taking a pair, which reuses the same element twice.
Forgetting p = 0: the answer is 0 even if the array is wide.

complexity.time: O(n log n + n log V), V = max − min

solutions.title: DP over the sorted array
solutions.idea: best[i][k] = smallest worst gap using the first i sorted values to make k pairs: either skip value i, or pair it with value i−1.

solutions.title: Binary search on the gap + greedy check
solutions.idea: For a limit D, greedily take neighbour pairs that fit. More D means more pairs, so binary search the smallest D giving p pairs.
solutions.time: O(n log n + n log V)

followups: Return the pairs themselves, not just the worst gap.
Instead of minimising the worst gap, minimise the sum of the p gaps. Does the greedy still work, or do you need the DP?
